FAQs
Key points to know before using Alpha.
What is Alpha Capital Group?

Alpha Capital Group is a UK prop firm. We run simulated evaluations so you can prove your strategy under clear rules. We are a proprietary trading company, not a broker. You pay for an evaluation. You do not deposit money to trade your own funds with us.

 Is Alpha Capital a prop firm traders can join?

Yes. Alpha Capital is a global prop firm available in 100+ countries — click here to view our complete country list. You buy an evaluation, trade simulated funds under the plan rules, and if you pass you can become a Qualified Analyst. From there you may earn performance fees based on results in our simulated environment. Nothing is guaranteed.

What is a prop firm?

A prop firm evaluates traders through a structured programme. At Alpha Capital that means a simulated trading environment, published risk rules, and a path to a Qualified Account if you pass. Performance fees are based on simulated results, not a promise of income.

Is Alpha Capital a broker?

No. We do not accept deposits for you to trade your own money. We are a proprietary trading company. You pay for the evaluation of your strategy in our simulated institutional execution environment.

Am I trading with real funds?

No. Evaluation accounts use simulated funds. After you pass, you stay in a simulated market environment as a Qualified Analyst. Eligible profits there can generate performance fees. Simulated results do not reflect real trading outcomes.

Do I need trading experience to start?

No prior experience is required to buy an evaluation. Passing without real trading skill is unlikely. Treat the evaluation like a serious test of your process, risk management, and consistency.

What happens after I pass the evaluation?

You move to a Qualified Account in our simulated environment. There is no profit target on that stage. You must keep following the risk rules for your plan. As a Qualified Analyst you can earn a 90% performance fee share on eligible profits.

What is the Alpha Group?

Alpha Capital sits in a wider group with Alpha Futures (futures prop evaluations), ACG Markets (the broker that powers our simulated institutional environment), and Alpha Prime (a progression path for top performers). Same group, different products.

What is Alpha Prime?

Alpha Prime is for skilled, consistent traders who progress from Alpha Capital or Alpha Futures. It is a separate London-based path with its own qualification routes and terms. It is not the same as a standard Qualified Account.

How do I get started with Alpha Capital?

Pick a plan and account size on our Product page, choose your platform, and complete checkout. After payment you get credentials and start trading under the published evaluation rules. Support runs Monday to Friday, 8am to 8pm GMT.

How Alpha Capital works in any country

Wherever you trade from, the model is identical. Alpha Capital runs evaluations on simulated accounts with simulated funds. These elements are the same in every supported country:

Evaluation paths: Alpha One (1-step), Alpha Pro (2-step), Alpha Swing (multi-day holds), Alpha Three (3-step) and Alpha Direct. Full figures are in the rules explained guide.

A valid government-issued photo ID (passport, driving licence, or national ID card). Paper-only ID is not accepted.
A selfie for facial matching.
The account holder must complete KYC personally, with no VPN or VPS during the process.

Alpha Pro 6% - Based on balance or equity, whichever is greater: 3%

The daily loss limit is determined based on the percentages above, calculated from your starting balance and/or equity for each trading day.

The starting balance and equity refer to the account balance and equity at the end of the trading day/beginning of the daily candle (broker time), which is 00:00 GMT+2.

 

Example for Alpha Pro 10% / Alpha Swing: 

If your account balance is $100,000 and your equity is $101,000 at the end of the daily candle, your maximum daily risk for the next day will be 5% of the starting balance ($100,000), resulting in a $5,000 maximum daily loss. This means your equity must remain above $95,000 at all times.

The open equity (including any floating gains or losses) from the previous trading day is not factored into the maximum daily loss calculation. Therefore, even if your balance is $100,000 and equity is $101,000, the minimum equity requirement remains $95,000. This allows for a theoretical loss of up to $6,000 during the day when considering floating unrealised profit or loss.

If your account balance is $100,000 and your equity is $99,000 at the close of the daily candle, the maximum daily risk for the following day will still be $5,000 (5% of the $100,000 starting balance). The minimum equity requirement remains $95,000. Thus, if you have open trades with a floating loss of -$1,000 carried over from the previous day, the maximum daily loss of $5,000 will be reduced by $1,000, since your equity is $99,000, and you will have $4,000 remaining in your maximum daily loss limit for that day.

 

Example for Alpha One 10% / Alpha Three: 

If your account balance is $100,000 and your equity is $101,000 at the end of the daily candle, your maximum daily risk for the next day will be 4% of the equity (since $101,000 equity is greater than the $100,000 balance). This results in a maximum daily loss of $4,040. Consequently, your minimum equity must remain above $96,960 (calculated as the equity at the start of the trading day, $101,000, minus the 4% maximum daily loss, $4,040).

 

If your account balance is $100,000 and your equity is $99,000 at the close of the daily candle, the maximum daily risk for the following day will be 4% of the balance (since the $100,000 balance is greater than the $99,000 equity). In this case, the minimum equity requirement will be $96,000 (calculated as the balance at the start of the trading day, $100,000, minus the 4% maximum daily loss, $4,000).

Best Day Rule

This rule states that no single trading day should contribute more than a set percentage of the total generated profits. This percentage depends on your plan:

Alpha Pro, Swing, One, and Three: 40%

Alpha Direct: 15%

Examples

Using the 40% threshold: if you earn $1,000 on a particular trading day, you will be eligible to request a withdrawal only once your account balance is more than $2,500 above its initial balance. This ensures that the $1,000 trading day accounts for less than 40% of the total profits in the account balance. Similarly, if your total profits are $4,000, your best day should be equal to or below $1,600 for you to be eligible to request a withdrawal.

For Alpha Direct, using the 15% threshold: on a $100,000 account, you first reach a 3% buffer ($3,000), then generate at least 1% more ($1,000) to request a payout, for $4,000 in total profit. In this example, your best day must stay at or below 15% of that total, so $600 or less ($4,000 x 15%). You then request a withdrawal of $1,000 above the buffer and receive $900 with Alpha Direct's 90% split.

 

More Information About the Consistency Score:

The consistency score is a simple calculation: the net profits generated on your best day are divided by the total net profits on the account.

 

If the result is greater than 0.40 (40%), the trader is not complying with the consistency rule. A trader becomes eligible once the result is 0.40 (40%) or less.

 

Real-life example: You receive your qualified account and generate $1,200 in net profit on day one. You continue trading, but no other trading day exceeds this $1,200 profit. Once your account balance is $3,000 above its initial balance, you are eligible to request a payout because your consistency score is exactly 40%:

 

1,200 ÷ 3,000 = 0.40 (40%)

 

Since the consistency score is 40% or less, the account meets the consistency rule requirements.

 

FAQ: 

My consistency is "0" – what does this mean?

This means your account is in drawdown. Since the net profit of your best day is being divided by a negative number (i.e. your account is currently at a loss), the result would technically be a negative number. However, we simply normalise the score to show as "0".

 

My consistency is above "100" – what does this mean?

This means that the net profit generated on your best day is greater than the total profit on the account. You will need to increase your total account profits so that the consistency score drops below the 40% threshold.

 

I made a certain amount of profit on my best day. How much profit do I need on the account to pass the consistency rule?

To find the required profit amount, simply multiply the net profit of your best trading day by 2.5. This works because 2.5 is the inverse of 40% (1 / 0.40), meaning the result of this calculation represents the minimum total profit your account must reach in order to meet the consistency rule and become eligible for a payout.

 

I want to withdraw partial profits. How will this affect my consistency?

When you make a partial withdrawal, your consistency score resets to 0, regardless of how much you leave in the account. This means you can request the remaining amount whenever you wish. However, once a new trade is placed, a new payout and consistency window starts.

 

For example, if you have made $1,000 and choose to withdraw $800, leaving $200 in the account, and you take another trade after the withdrawal, from that point on, the consistency will be based on the current payout window alone. This means the $200 will be "locked" until you fulfil the requirements.

 

Say, for example, that on Day 1 of this payout window, you make $1,000 in net profit. If no other trading day surpasses this amount, you will need to profit $2,500 within this payout window in order to pass consistency. However, note that once the account balance is $2,500 above its initial balance, you still cannot request your withdrawal, as $200 of it is from the previous payout window.

 

Here is how the system interprets it:

 

- Best day of this payout window: $1,000

- Profits made in this payout window: $2,300 (account balance is $2,500 above its initial balance, but $200 is from the previous window)

- Consistency score: 1,000 / 2,300 = 43%, therefore not compliant with the rule

 

The account balance must be more than $2,700 above its initial balance for you to request a withdrawal; that is $1,000 (best day) × 2.5 = $2,500 (required profit), plus the $200 that remained from the previous window.

 

To summarise:

- A partial withdrawal resets consistency; you can request the remaining amount whenever you want.

Key rules that close accounts
Maximum drawdown

If your balance falls below the drawdown floor, the account closes. Static drawdown is fixed from your initial balance and never moves. Trailing drawdown (Alpha One) follows your high-water mark and then locks at the initial balance once you are up by the drawdown percentage (6% on One 10%), as explained above. See trailing vs static drawdown.

Daily loss limit

The maximum you can lose in one trading day, measured from the start of the daily candle (00:00 GMT+3). On Alpha One, Alpha Three, and Alpha Pro 6%, it is based on the higher of that day's starting balance or equity. On Alpha Pro 8%, Alpha Pro 10%, and Alpha Swing, it is balance-based. Either way, a breach is judged on your live equity, so open (unrealised) losses count, not just closed trades.

Max Risk Rule

The Max Risk Rule applies to Qualified Accounts bought after 21 July 2026. It limits open drawdown, meaning floating losses, on any one asset. The limit is 3% on $5,000 to $25,000 accounts, 2% on $50,000 to $200,000 accounts, and 1% on Alpha Direct at all sizes. Each asset is tracked separately, and the first one to reach its limit closes the account, however your other positions are doing.

Losing positions on the same asset are combined, and profitable ones do not offset them. All trading costs, including commissions, swaps and slippage, count towards the limit, so leave a buffer below it.

If you close a trade and open a new one on the same asset, in the same direction, within 10 minutes, the losses from both trades count together towards the limit. This carries on with each further trade, so a run of quick re-entries can form one continuous chain. The chain only ends once more than 10 minutes pass between one trade closing and the next one opening. Switching direction does not end it, because trades the other way on the same asset form a separate chain.

Minimum trading days

Alpha One requires 1 trading day. Alpha Pro, Alpha Swing, and Alpha Three require 3 per phase. A trading day counts when you open and close at least one position.

30-day inactivity

If no trade is placed for 30 consecutive days, the account is deactivated. This applies to all accounts in all stages, so keep the account active even while waiting for a setup.

Minimum trade duration (anti-HFT)

Alpha Capital expects a genuine trading style, not latency or high-frequency exploitation of the simulated feed. Your average trade duration must be above 2 minutes, and at least 50% of your profit (targeted profit during evaluations, gross profit on a Qualified Account) must come from trades held longer than 2 minutes. Occasional individual trades under 2 minutes are fine. This rule applies to all accounts. See prohibited trading strategies for the full compliance list. For what counts as hedging and how Alpha Capital treats it, see what hedging is in trading.

The 40% Best Day Rule

If you request performance fees on-demand, no single trading day can represent more than 40% of your total cumulative profit. Example: if you have $10,000 cumulative profit and your best day produced $4,500 (45%), you cannot request on-demand yet. It does not apply to bi-weekly schedules. Common mistakes that breach accounts
Misreading Alpha One trailing. On One 10%, once you are up 6%, the floor is your starting balance, not a moving 6% below your peak. Plan your buffer around that.
Forgetting unrealised losses. Open drawdown counts toward your daily limit. Watch equity, not just closed P&L.
Stacking size into news. One bad release can erase a daily limit in seconds. Treat news as volatility, not opportunity to size up.
Not counting trading days correctly. Count days where you completed at least one round trip, not calendar days.
Leaving the account dormant. 30 days without a trade closes it.

Prop Firm Terminology (Evaluation vs Challenge)

Search engines and forums mix labels. On Alpha Capital’s site, these terms map like this:

Trading evaluation = what many traders call a prop firm challenge or funded trader challenge
Qualified trader = often called a funded trader elsewhere
Performance fee = commonly called a payout
Performance split = profit split on eligible simulated profits

Throughout this page, evaluation means the paid assessment. Where we mention “challenge”, it refers to how other firms or traders describe the same step — not an Alpha Capital product label.

What Is a Prop Firm Evaluation Fee?

An evaluation fee is the one-time price you pay to attempt qualification at a proprietary trading firm. It covers platform access, published drawdown rules, profit targets, and support for that assessment period. If you pass, you may become a qualified trader — often called a funded trader in other communities — and request performance fees on eligible simulated profits.

At most retail prop programmes — including Alpha Capital — your direct financial exposure is typically the evaluation fee plus any optional resets, not the full nominal account size ($100K simulated does not mean you deposited $100K).

Wie Alpha Capital funktioniert in jedem Land

Egal von wo Sie handeln, das Modell ist identisch.. Alpha Capital Führt Bewertungen auf simulierten Konten mit virtuellem Kapital durch. Sie zahlen eine Bewertungsgebühr, handeln über eine oder mehrere Bewertungs-Phasen und wenn Sie die Gewinnziele ohne Verstoß gegen die Regeln erreichen, gelangen Sie zu einem qualifizierten Konto, auf dem Sie Performance-Gebühren für Ihre simulierten Gewinne verdienen können.

Diese Elemente sind in jedem unterstützten Land gleich:

Bewertungs-Pfade: Alpha One (1-Schritt), Alpha Pro (2-stufig), Alpha Swing (mehrtägige Positionen), Alpha Three (3-stufig) und Alpha Direct. Vollständige Zahlen sind in der Regeln erklärt Anleitung.
Konten-Größen: von $2.500 (Alpha Direct) bis zu $200.000 simulierten Konten, je nach Plan.
Kontowährung: Alles ist in US-Dollar (USD) preisgebunden und dimensioniert. Ein „$100.000-Konto“ ist ein $100.000-Simulationskonto, kein echtes Geld und kein lokales Währungskonto. Wenn Sie mit einer lokalen Karte bezahlen, wickelt Ihre Bank die Konvertierung ab.
Brokerageumgebung: Bewertungshandel läuft durch Alpha Capital Partners ACG Markets in einer simulierten institutionellen Umgebung.
Performance-Split: 80 % der simulierten Gewinne als Standard, bis zu 90 % mit dem Add-on bei Alpha One und bei Alpha Pro auf Anfrage oder als Standard bei Alpha Direct. Ausgezahlt wird zweiwöchentlich oder auf Anfrage je nach Programm, innerhalb von 2 Werktagen.
Performance-Gebührenmodelle: Rise, Wise, Banküberweisung (WIRE / ACH / SWIFT), oder Kryptowährungen über Rise (nicht direkt in Kryptowährungen ausgezahlt).
Zahlungen muss auf den Namen des Karteninhabers lauten. Zahlungen mit Karten oder Konten Dritter werden nicht akzeptiert, und der Zahlungsname wird mit Ihrem Identitätsprofil abgeglichen.
Identitätsprüfung (KYC), überall

Bevor ein qualifiziertes Konto ausgestellt wird oder eine Performance-Gebühr gezahlt wird, führen Sie eine KYC-Prüfung durch. Dies gilt in jedem Land.

Ein gültiger, amtlich ausgestellter Lichtbildausweis (Reisepass, Führerschein oder Personalausweis). Papiere Ausweise werden nicht akzeptiert.
Ein Selfie zur Gesichtserkennung.
